# Rinda — Complete Documentation

> Rinda is a managed Queue-as-a-Service platform that wraps cloud queue services
> (AWS SQS, Azure Service Bus) and provides an easy-to-use SDK, REST API, and web dashboard.
> No cloud credentials or infrastructure knowledge required.

---

# Quickstart

Get up and running with Rinda in under 5 minutes. By the end of this guide you'll have created a queue, sent a message, and received it.

## Prerequisites

- A [Rinda account](https://app.rinda.dev) (free tier available)
- An API key (create one in **Settings > API Keys**)

## 1. Install the SDK


  ### npm

```bash
npm install @rindahq/sdk
```

  
  ### pnpm

```bash
pnpm add @rindahq/sdk
```

  
  ### Yarn

```bash
yarn add @rindahq/sdk
```

  
  ### Bun

```bash
bun add @rindahq/sdk
```

  


 Looking for another language?
We currently offer an official SDK for Node.js/TypeScript. For Python, PHP, C#, Go, and other languages, use the [REST API](/docs/api-reference/rinda-api) directly with any HTTP client — it works with any language that can make HTTP requests.


## 2. Create a Queue


  ### Node.js SDK

```typescript

const rinda = new Rinda({
  apiKey: 'rk_prod_your_api_key',
});

const queue = await rinda.queues.create({
  name: 'order-events',
  region: 'us-east-1',
});

console.log('Queue created:', queue.id);
```

  
  ### REST API

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.rinda.dev/v1/queues \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer rk_prod_your_api_key" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name": "order-events", "region": "us-east-1"}'
```

  


## 3. Send a Message


  ### Node.js SDK

```typescript
const q = rinda.queue(queue.id);

const { messageId } = await q.send({
  body: { orderId: '123', status: 'confirmed' },
});

console.log('Message sent:', messageId);
```

  
  ### REST API

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.rinda.dev/v1/queues/QUEUE_ID/messages \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer rk_prod_your_api_key" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"body": {"orderId": "123", "status": "confirmed"}}'
```

  


## 4. Receive Messages


  ### Node.js SDK

```typescript
const messages = await q.receive({
  maxMessages: 10,
  waitTimeSeconds: 20, // Long-polling
});

for (const msg of messages) {
  console.log('Received:', msg.body);
  await msg.delete(); // Acknowledge the message
}
```

  
  ### REST API

```bash
# Receive messages (long-poll for 20 seconds)
curl "https://api.rinda.dev/v1/queues/QUEUE_ID/messages?maxMessages=10&waitTimeSeconds=20" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer rk_prod_your_api_key"

# Delete (acknowledge) a message
curl -X DELETE "https://api.rinda.dev/v1/queues/QUEUE_ID/messages/MESSAGE_ID" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer rk_prod_your_api_key"
```

  


## 5. Use Workers (SDK)

The SDK includes a `QueueWorker` that automatically polls for messages with retry logic and graceful shutdown:

```typescript

const rinda = new Rinda({ apiKey: 'rk_prod_your_api_key' });
const q = rinda.queue('QUEUE_ID');

const worker = q.createWorker({
  handler: async (message) => {
    console.log('Processing:', message.body);
    // Your processing logic here
    return message; // Acknowledge — message is auto-deleted
  },
  batchSize: 5,
  waitTimeSeconds: 20,
});

worker.start();

// Graceful shutdown
process.on('SIGTERM', () => worker.stop());
```

## Next Steps

- [Authentication](/docs/getting-started/authentication) — Learn about API keys and scoping
- [Core Concepts](/docs/getting-started/concepts) — Understand projects, environments, and queues
- [Queues Guide](/docs/guides/queues) — Deep dive into queue configuration
- [FIFO Queues](/docs/guides/fifo-queues) — Strict ordering and exactly-once delivery
- [Message Storage](/docs/guides/storage) — large message bodies, and the archive of what you sent
- [API Reference](/docs/api-reference/rinda-api) — Full API documentation with code examples

# Authentication

All Rinda API requests require authentication via an API key passed as a Bearer token.

## API Keys

API keys are prefixed with `rk_` followed by the environment identifier:

| Prefix | Environment |
|--------|-------------|
| `rk_prod_...` | Production |
| `rk_stg_...` | Staging |
| `rk_dev_...` | Development |

### Creating an API Key

1. Log in to the [Rinda Dashboard](https://app.rinda.dev)
2. Navigate to **Settings > API Keys**
3. Click **Create API Key**
4. Give it a descriptive name (e.g., "backend-service")
5. Copy the key — it is only shown once

### Using Your API Key


  ### Node.js SDK

```typescript

const rinda = new Rinda({
  apiKey: process.env.RINDA_API_KEY, // rk_prod_...
});
```

  
  ### REST API

```bash
curl https://api.rinda.dev/v1/queues \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $RINDA_API_KEY"
```

Works with any HTTP client in any language — just set the `Authorization: Bearer <key>` header.

  


## Environment scoping

Each API key belongs to one **project** and one **environment**. A production
key cannot reach staging queues, or the other way round.

## Permissions

By default a key can do anything its plan allows. On a paid plan you can narrow
that when creating the key:

| Preset | What it can do |
|---|---|
| **Full access** | Everything |
| **Read only** | Receive messages, list and inspect queues |
| **Write only** | Send messages, create and configure queues |
| **Custom** | Any combination of the individual permissions |

The individual permissions are `queues:read`, `queues:write`, `messages:read`,
and `messages:write`. A request outside a key's permissions is refused with
`403` and a body naming the permission that was missing:

```json
{
  "error": {
    "code": "insufficient_scope",
    "message": "This API key cannot perform this action.",
    "required": "messages:write",
    "granted": ["messages:read", "queues:read"]
  }
}
```

A key issued before permissions existed has none recorded and keeps full
access, so nothing breaks on upgrade.

## Expiry

On a paid plan a key can be given an expiry — 30, 90, or 365 days. After that
it stops authenticating. A key with no expiry never lapses.

## Rotating a key without downtime

Rotation issues a replacement and keeps the old key working for an overlap
window, so there is no moment when neither key is valid:

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.rinda.dev/v1/api-keys/{keyId}/rotate \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $RINDA_SESSION" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"overlapHours": 24}'
```

```json
{
  "key": "rk_prod_the_new_key_shown_once",
  "name": "Production Key",
  "replaced": { "prefix": "rk_prod_a1b2c3", "expiresAt": "2026-08-26T12:00:00Z" }
}
```

The replacement carries the same permissions, environment, and expiry policy.
The sequence is:

1. Rotate. Both keys work.
2. Deploy the new key.
3. The old key expires at the end of the overlap — no action needed.

Both keys count against your plan's per-environment key limit during the
overlap, so rotation needs a free slot. The Free tier allows one key per
environment and therefore cannot rotate without a gap; paid plans allow three
or more.

Rotation is not the same as revoking. **Revoking** cuts a key off immediately —
right for a leaked key, wrong for a planned replacement.

## Security practices

- **Never commit keys.** Use environment variables.
- **Give each service its own key**, so one can be revoked without affecting
  the others.
- **Narrow the permissions.** A service that only consumes needs `messages:read`.
- **Rotate on a schedule** using the overlap above, rather than revoking and
  scrambling to redeploy.
- **Use environment-specific keys.** Never a production key in development.

## Error Responses

If authentication fails, the API returns a `401 Unauthorized` response:

```json
{
  "statusCode": 401,
  "message": "Unauthorized",
  "error": "Invalid or missing API key"
}
```

---

# Core Concepts

This page explains the key building blocks of Rinda and how they relate to each other.

## Architecture Overview

```
Account
  └── Project
       └── Environment (dev / staging / production)
            ├── Queues
            │    └── Messages
            └── Storage Objects
```

## Account

Your Rinda account is the top-level container. Each account has:

- A **billing subscription** (Free, Scale, or Dedicated)
- One or more **projects**
- **Per-account encryption** — every account gets its own encryption key

## Projects

A project groups related queues and storage objects together. Think of it as a workspace for a single application or microservice.

- Each project has its own set of **environments**
- Queues and storage are isolated per project

## Environments

Each project comes with three environments out of the box:

| Environment | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Development** | Local development and testing |
| **Staging** | Pre-production validation |
| **Production** | Live traffic |

API keys are scoped to an environment, so your dev code can never accidentally write to production queues.

## Queues

A queue is a message channel. Rinda supports two types:

### Standard Queues
- **Best-effort ordering** — messages are generally delivered in order, but not guaranteed
- **At-least-once delivery** — messages may be delivered more than once
- **Higher throughput** — no ordering constraints

### FIFO Queues
- **Strict ordering** — messages are delivered in the exact order they were sent
- **Exactly-once processing** — message deduplication prevents duplicates
- **Message groups** — independent ordering within groups

## Messages

Messages are the data you send through queues. Key properties:

| Property | Description |
|---|---|
| **body** | Any JSON payload (up to 190 KB inline, 1 MB stored) |
| **delaySeconds** | Delay before the message becomes visible (0-900s) |
| **visibilityTimeout** | Time a message stays invisible after being received |
| **groupId** | Message group for FIFO ordering |
| **deduplicationId** | Prevents duplicate messages in FIFO queues |

### Message Lifecycle

```
Sent → Pending → Received (invisible) → Deleted (acknowledged)
                      │
                      └→ Visible again (if not deleted within visibility timeout)
                              │
                              └→ Dead Letter Queue (after max retries)
```

### Large Messages

Messages over 190 KB are automatically stored in Rinda Storage and a reference pointer is sent through the queue. This is transparent — you always receive the full message body.

## Message Storage

Rinda keeps message bodies so that:

- **Large payloads** can be sent at all — a body over the queue's limit is
  stored, and a reference travels on the queue
- **Messages can be inspected** long after they were processed
- **Messages can be replayed**, using the body exactly as it was sent

How long they are kept is set per account. See
[Message Storage](/docs/guides/storage).

## Dead Letter Queues (DLQ)

When a message fails to be processed after a configurable number of attempts, it is automatically moved to a dead-letter queue for investigation. DLQ can be enabled per queue with a single toggle.

## Next Steps

- [Quickstart](/docs/getting-started/quickstart) — Send your first message
- [Queues Guide](/docs/guides/queues) — Deep dive into queue configuration
- [API Reference](/docs/api-reference/rinda-api) — Full API documentation

---

# Queues

Queues are the core building block of Rinda. A queue holds messages until they are consumed by your application.

## Creating a Queue


  ### Node.js SDK

```typescript

const rinda = new Rinda({ apiKey: 'rk_prod_your_api_key' });

const queue = await rinda.queues.create({
  name: 'order-events',
  region: 'us-east-1',
});

console.log('Queue created:', queue.id, queue.name);
```

  
  ### REST API

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.rinda.dev/v1/queues \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $RINDA_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "name": "order-events",
    "region": "us-east-1"
  }'
```

  


## Queue Types

### Standard Queues

Best for high-throughput workloads where strict ordering is not required:

- Messages delivered at least once
- Best-effort ordering
- Nearly unlimited throughput

### FIFO Queues

Best for workflows that require strict message ordering:

- Messages delivered in exact order
- Exactly-once processing via deduplication
- Message groups for parallel ordered processing

```typescript
const fifoQueue = await rinda.queues.create({
  name: 'payment-events',
  region: 'us-east-1',
  isFifo: true,
  dlqEnabled: true,
  maxReceiveCount: 3,
});
```

See the [FIFO Queues Guide](/docs/guides/fifo-queues) for details.

## Configuration Options

| Option | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | *required* | Unique name within the project |
| `region` | *required* | Region the queue runs in (`us-east-1`, `eu-west-1`, etc.) |
| `isFifo` | `false` | Create a FIFO queue for strict ordering |
| `encrypted` | `true` | Enable server-side encryption |
| `dlqEnabled` | `false` | Enable dead-letter queue |
| `maxReceiveCount` | `5` | Max delivery attempts before sending to DLQ |
| `visibilityTimeoutSecs` | `30` | Seconds a message stays invisible after being received |
| `messageRetentionDays` | `4` | Days to retain unprocessed messages |
| `delaySeconds` | `0` | Default delay for messages in this queue |

## Listing Queues

```typescript
const queues = await rinda.queues.list();
for (const q of queues) {
  console.log(`${q.name} (${q.isFifo ? 'FIFO' : 'standard'}) — ${q.region}`);
}
```

## Getting a Queue

```typescript
const queue = await rinda.queues.get('QUEUE_ID');
console.log(queue.name, queue.isFifo, queue.region);
```

## Queue Statistics

```typescript
const q = rinda.queue('QUEUE_ID');

const stats = await q.stats();
console.log('Messages available:', stats.approximateMessageCount);
console.log('Messages in flight:', stats.approximateNotVisible);
console.log('Messages delayed:', stats.approximateDelayed);
```

## Deleting a Queue


Deleting a queue permanently removes all its messages. This action cannot be undone.


```typescript
await rinda.queues.delete('QUEUE_ID');
```

## Regions

| Region | Location |
|---|---|
| `us-east-1` | N. Virginia |
| `us-west-2` | Oregon |
| `eu-west-1` | Ireland |
| `eu-central-1` | Frankfurt |
| `ap-southeast-1` | Singapore |

## Backlog alerts

A queue filling faster than it drains is invisible until something downstream
breaks, and by then the backlog is hours old. Set a threshold and the account
owners are emailed when it is crossed:

```typescript
await rinda.queues.update('QUEUE_ID', { depthAlertThreshold: 1000 });
```

Or from the queue's **Settings** page in the dashboard.

The count includes messages being retried, not just ones waiting to be picked
up — a queue whose consumer keeps failing has everything in flight, and
counting only what is visible would call it empty.

### One email per backlog

You get one email when the queue crosses the threshold, and no more until it
drops back under and rises again. An alert that repeats every fifteen minutes
until someone fixes it is one people build a mail filter for, and then the
next one goes unread too.

Recovery is not emailed either. A queue draining is the expected outcome, and
mail nobody has to act on trains people to ignore the mail they do.

### Turning it off

```typescript
await rinda.queues.update('QUEUE_ID', { depthAlertThreshold: null });
```

There is no default threshold. What counts as backed up depends entirely on
the queue — ten messages is an emergency on one that is normally empty and
unremarkable on one that batches overnight — so nothing is watched until you
say what to watch for.

---

# Messages

Messages are the data you push through Rinda queues. This guide covers all message operations.

## Sending Messages

### Single Message


  ### Node.js SDK

```typescript
const q = rinda.queue('QUEUE_ID');

const { messageId } = await q.send({
  body: { orderId: '123', action: 'process' },
});

console.log('Message ID:', messageId);
```

  
  ### REST API

```bash
curl -X POST "https://api.rinda.dev/v1/queues/QUEUE_ID/messages" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $RINDA_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"body": {"orderId": "123", "action": "process"}}'
```

  


### Batch Send (up to 10)

```typescript
const result = await q.sendBatch([
  { body: { orderId: '1' } },
  { body: { orderId: '2' } },
  { body: { orderId: '3' } },
]);

console.log('Sent:', result.messageIds); // ['msg-id-1', 'msg-id-2', 'msg-id-3']
```

### Delayed Messages

```typescript
await q.send({
  body: { reminder: 'Follow up in 5 minutes' },
  delaySeconds: 300, // Message becomes visible after 5 minutes
});
```

### Message Attributes

Attach custom metadata to messages:

```typescript
await q.send({
  body: { orderId: '123' },
  attributes: {
    source: 'checkout-service',
    priority: 'high',
  },
});
```

## Receiving Messages

### Basic Receive


  ### Node.js SDK

```typescript
const messages = await q.receive({
  maxMessages: 10,       // Receive up to 10 messages
  waitTimeSeconds: 20,   // Long-poll for up to 20 seconds (the default)
});
```

  
  ### REST API

```bash
curl "https://api.rinda.dev/v1/queues/QUEUE_ID/messages?maxMessages=10&waitTimeSeconds=20" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $RINDA_API_KEY"
```

  


### Long Polling

Receiving long-polls by default: with no `waitTimeSeconds`, the call waits up
to **20 seconds** for a message to arrive and returns as soon as one does.
This is what you want almost always — a consumer that short-polls spends most
of its requests being told there is nothing, and each of those round trips
costs latency for work it did not do.

```typescript
// Both wait up to 20 seconds.
const messages = await q.receive();
const same = await q.receive({ waitTimeSeconds: 20 });
```

Twenty seconds is the maximum; anything higher is clamped to it.

Pass `0` when you want the opposite — an answer now, empty or not. That suits
draining a queue in a loop, or a health check that must not block:

```typescript
const messages = await q.receive({ waitTimeSeconds: 0 });
```


The AWS SDK compatibility endpoint keeps SQS's default of `0` rather than this
one, because it emulates SQS rather than replacing it.


### Processing and Acknowledging

After processing a message, delete it to acknowledge receipt:

```typescript
for (const msg of messages) {
  try {
    await processOrder(msg.body);
    await msg.delete(); // Acknowledge
  } catch (error) {
    // Don't delete — message becomes visible again after timeout
    console.error('Processing failed:', error);
  }
}
```

Each received message includes useful metadata:

```typescript
for (const msg of messages) {
  console.log('ID:', msg.id);
  console.log('Body:', msg.body);
  console.log('Receive count:', msg.approximateReceiveCount);
  console.log('Received at:', msg.receivedAt);
}
```

## Deleting Messages

### By Message ID

Delete a message by its ID, without needing the receipt handle from a receive:

```typescript
await q.remove('MESSAGE_ID');
```

## Large Messages

Messages up to **190 KB** travel on the queue itself. Larger bodies, up to
**1 MB**, are stored by Rinda and a reference travels on the queue instead.

The queue engine underneath caps a message at 256 KB counting its attributes,
and a stored body is encrypted before it is written — which costs a little
more than the body itself. 190 KB is the largest payload that fits inside
both of those with room to spare, so the limit does not move underneath you.

This is fully transparent: send and receive look the same at any size, and
ordering, deduplication, delivery counts, and dead-letter behaviour are
unaffected.

```typescript
const q = rinda.queue('QUEUE_ID');

// Send a payload larger than 190 KB — stored, with a reference on the queue
const largePayload = { data: 'x'.repeat(300 * 1024), type: 'report' };
const { messageId } = await q.send({ body: largePayload });

// Receive — the full body comes back, not a reference
const messages = await q.receive({ maxMessages: 1, waitTimeSeconds: 5 });
console.log(messages[0].body.type); // 'report'
console.log(messages[0].body.data.length); // 307200
await messages[0].delete();
```

## Visibility Timeout

When a message is received, it becomes invisible to other consumers for the visibility timeout period. If the message is not deleted within this time, it becomes visible again for reprocessing.

## Error Handling

```typescript

try {
  await q.send({ body: { orderId: '123' } });
} catch (error) {
  if (error instanceof RindaApiError) {
    console.error('API error:', error.message);
    console.error('Status:', error.statusCode);
    console.error('Request ID:', error.requestId);
  }
}
```

---

# Message Storage

Rinda stores message bodies that are too large to travel on the queue itself,
and keeps an archive of the messages you send so you can inspect and replay
them later.

It is not a general-purpose file store. Nothing uploads to it directly — Rinda
writes to it on your behalf when you send a message.

## Large messages

A queue caps a message body at 190 KB. Send something larger and Rinda stores
the body and puts a reference on the queue; on receive it swaps the reference
back for your payload. Your code does not change:

```typescript
// 400 KB — over the queue limit, and it just works.
await rinda.queue('orders').send({ body: { report: bigJsonBlob } });

const [message] = await rinda.queue('orders').receive();
console.log(message.body.report); // the full payload, not a reference
```

A single body is capped at 1 MB. Past that the send is rejected rather than
stored — at that size you want your own storage and a reference in the message,
rather than a queue carrying the payload.

Nothing else about the message changes: ordering, deduplication, delivery
counts, and dead-letter behaviour work the same whether the body travelled on
the queue or beside it.

## Inspecting and replaying

Every message you send is recorded, so you can look at what was actually sent
long after it was processed — including bodies that were too large for the
queue. Find them under **Storage** in the dashboard, or on a queue's
**Messages** tab.

How much Rinda keeps depends on the queue's persistence setting:

| Setting | What is kept |
|---|---|
| `NONE` | Only bodies too large to send inline — those must be stored to be sent at all |
| `LARGE_ONLY` *(default)* | Large bodies, plus a short preview of every other message |
| `ALL` | Every message body in full |

## Retention

Archived bodies are kept for a window set per account:

| Plan | Window |
|---|---|
| Free | 7 days, fixed |
| Scale and Dedicated | 7, 15, 30, or 60 days |

Change it under **Settings → Retention**. Expiry is asynchronous, so the
guarantee is "kept for **at least** the window", not "deleted the instant it
elapses".

Shortening the window deletes anything already past it, and downgrading a plan
narrows the window to what the new plan allows — that data does not come back
by upgrading again.

---

# Workers

The `QueueWorker` class in the Rinda SDK provides a reliable, production-ready message consumer with automatic polling, error handling, and graceful shutdown.

## Creating a Worker

Create a worker from a queue handle:

```typescript

const rinda = new Rinda({ apiKey: process.env.RINDA_API_KEY });
const q = rinda.queue('QUEUE_ID');

const worker = q.createWorker({
  handler: async (message) => {
    console.log('Processing:', message.body);
    // Your processing logic here
    return message; // Acknowledge — message is auto-deleted
  },
});

worker.start();
console.log('Worker running:', worker.isRunning); // true
```

## Configuration Options

```typescript
const worker = q.createWorker({
  handler: async (message) => {
    await processOrder(message.body);
    return message;
  },
  batchSize: 5,            // Messages per poll (1-10, default: 1)
  visibilityTimeout: 60,   // Seconds before message reappears (default: 30)
  waitTimeSeconds: 20,     // Long-poll duration (0-20, default: 20)
  pollingWaitTimeMs: 0,    // Delay between polls in ms (default: 0)
  shouldDeleteMessages: true, // Auto-delete on success (default: true)
});
```

| Option | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `handler` | — | Async function to process a single message |
| `batchHandler` | — | Async function to process a batch of messages |
| `batchSize` | `1` / `10` | Messages per poll (1 for handler, 10 for batchHandler) |
| `visibilityTimeout` | `30` | Seconds before unacknowledged message reappears |
| `waitTimeSeconds` | `20` | Long-poll wait time in seconds |
| `pollingWaitTimeMs` | `0` | Delay between polling cycles in ms |
| `shouldDeleteMessages` | `true` | Auto-delete messages after successful processing |


Provide either `handler` (single message) or `batchHandler` (batch), not both.


## Batch Handler

Process multiple messages at once for higher throughput:

```typescript
const worker = q.createWorker({
  batchHandler: async (messages) => {
    console.log(`Processing batch of ${messages.length} message(s)`);

    for (const msg of messages) {
      await processOrder(msg.body);
    }

    return messages; // Acknowledge all
  },
  batchSize: 10,
});

worker.start();
```

## Error Handling

If the handler throws an error, the message is **not deleted** and becomes visible again after the visibility timeout:

```typescript
const worker = q.createWorker({
  handler: async (message) => {
    const order = message.body;

    if (!order.id) {
      throw new Error('Invalid order — missing ID');
      // Message will be retried, eventually going to DLQ
    }

    await processOrder(order);
    return message; // Auto-deleted on success
  },
});
```

## Worker Events

Listen for lifecycle events:

```typescript
const worker = q.createWorker({ handler });

worker.on('message_received', (msg) => {
  console.log('Received:', msg.id);
});

worker.on('message_processed', (msg) => {
  console.log('Processed:', msg.id);
});

worker.on('processing_error', (err, msg) => {
  console.error('Failed:', msg.id, err.message);
});

worker.on('error', (err) => {
  console.error('Worker error:', err);
});

worker.on('empty', () => {
  console.log('Queue is empty');
});

worker.start();
```

## Graceful Shutdown

Stop the worker gracefully to finish processing in-flight messages:

```typescript
const worker = q.createWorker({ handler });
worker.start();

// Handle shutdown signals
process.on('SIGTERM', () => {
  console.log('Shutting down worker...');
  worker.stop(); // Finishes in-flight messages
});

process.on('SIGINT', () => {
  worker.stop();
});
```

## Multiple Workers

Run multiple workers for different queues or parallel processing:

```typescript
const orderQueue = rinda.queue('ORDER_QUEUE_ID');
const notificationQueue = rinda.queue('NOTIFICATION_QUEUE_ID');

const orderWorker = orderQueue.createWorker({
  handler: processOrder,
  batchSize: 5,
});

const notificationWorker = notificationQueue.createWorker({
  handler: sendNotification,
  batchSize: 10,
});

orderWorker.start();
notificationWorker.start();
```

## Best Practices

1. **Use long-polling** — Set `waitTimeSeconds: 20` to minimize API calls and cost
2. **Enable DLQ** — Configure dead-letter queues so failed messages don't block the queue
3. **Handle signals** — Always implement graceful shutdown to avoid message loss
4. **Keep handlers idempotent** — Messages may be delivered more than once (standard queues)
5. **Set appropriate visibility timeouts** — Match to your expected processing time plus buffer
6. **Return the message** — Always `return message` (or `return messages` for batch) to acknowledge successful processing

---

# FIFO Queues

FIFO (First-In-First-Out) queues guarantee that messages are processed in the exact order they are sent, with exactly-once delivery semantics.

## Creating a FIFO Queue


  ### Node.js SDK

```typescript
const queue = await rinda.queues.create({
  name: 'payment-events',
  region: 'us-east-1',
  isFifo: true,
  dlqEnabled: true,
  maxReceiveCount: 3,
});

console.log('FIFO queue:', queue.id, queue.isFifo); // true
```

  
  ### REST API

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.rinda.dev/v1/queues \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $RINDA_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "name": "payment-events",
    "region": "us-east-1",
    "isFifo": true,
    "dlqEnabled": true,
    "maxReceiveCount": 3
  }'
```

  


## Message Groups

Message groups allow parallel processing while maintaining order within each group. Use `groupId` to assign messages to a group:

```typescript
const q = rinda.queue(queue.id, { isFifo: true });

// Messages for customer-123 are processed in order
await q.send({
  body: { action: 'charge', amount: 99.99 },
  groupId: 'customer-123',
  deduplicationId: 'charge-001',
});

await q.send({
  body: { action: 'refund', amount: 99.99 },
  groupId: 'customer-123',
  deduplicationId: 'refund-001',
});

// Different group — processed independently and in parallel
await q.send({
  body: { action: 'charge', amount: 49.99 },
  groupId: 'customer-456',
  deduplicationId: 'charge-002',
});
```

## Batch Send

Send multiple FIFO messages at once. Every message must include `groupId` and `deduplicationId`:

```typescript
const q = rinda.queue(queue.id, { isFifo: true });

const result = await q.sendBatch([
  { body: { seq: 1 }, groupId: 'batch-group', deduplicationId: 'dedup-1' },
  { body: { seq: 2 }, groupId: 'batch-group', deduplicationId: 'dedup-2' },
  { body: { seq: 3 }, groupId: 'batch-group', deduplicationId: 'dedup-3' },
]);

console.log('Sent:', result.messageIds.length, 'messages');
```

## Receiving FIFO Messages

Receive and process messages in order:

```typescript
const q = rinda.queue(queue.id);

const messages = await q.receive({ maxMessages: 5 });
for (const msg of messages) {
  console.log('Body:', msg.body);
  await msg.delete();
}
```

## Deduplication

The `deduplicationId` prevents duplicate messages within a 5-minute window:

```typescript
await q.send({
  body: { orderId: '123' },
  groupId: 'orders',
  deduplicationId: 'order-123-created',
});

// This is a no-op — same deduplicationId within the dedup window
await q.send({
  body: { orderId: '123' },
  groupId: 'orders',
  deduplicationId: 'order-123-created',
});
```

## SDK Validation

When you create a queue handle with `{ isFifo: true }`, the SDK validates that `groupId` and `deduplicationId` are provided before sending:

```typescript

const q = rinda.queue(queue.id, { isFifo: true });

try {
  // Throws — missing groupId and deduplicationId
  await q.send({ body: { test: true } });
} catch (err) {
  if (err instanceof RindaValidationError) {
    console.error(err.message); // 'FIFO queues require "groupId"...'
  }
}
```

Batch validation reports the specific index:

```typescript
try {
  await q.sendBatch([
    { body: { a: 1 }, groupId: 'g1', deduplicationId: 'd1' },
    { body: { b: 2 } }, // Missing groupId at index 1
  ]);
} catch (err) {
  console.error(err.message); // '...Missing on message at index 1.'
}
```

## FIFO Queue Stats

```typescript
const q = rinda.queue(queue.id);
const stats = await q.stats();
console.log('Messages:', stats.approximateMessageCount);
```

## When to Use FIFO

| Use Case | Queue Type |
|---|---|
| Event processing where order matters | FIFO |
| Financial transactions | FIFO |
| State machine updates | FIFO |
| Log ingestion | Standard |
| Email notifications | Standard |
| Thumbnail generation | Standard |

## Limitations

- FIFO queues have lower throughput than standard queues (300 messages/second per group)
- Both `groupId` and `deduplicationId` are required for every message
- Deduplication window is 5 minutes

---

# Dead Letter Queues

A Dead Letter Queue (DLQ) captures messages that fail to be processed after a configurable number of attempts, preventing them from blocking the main queue.

## Enabling DLQ

Enable DLQ when creating a queue by setting `dlqEnabled` and `maxReceiveCount`:

```typescript
const queue = await rinda.queues.create({
  name: 'order-events',
  region: 'us-east-1',
  dlqEnabled: true,
  maxReceiveCount: 5, // Move to DLQ after 5 failed attempts
});

console.log('DLQ enabled:', queue.dlqEnabled); // true
```

This works for both standard and FIFO queues:

```typescript
const fifoQueue = await rinda.queues.create({
  name: 'payment-events',
  region: 'us-east-1',
  isFifo: true,
  dlqEnabled: true,
  maxReceiveCount: 3,
});
```

## How It Works

```
Message sent → Queue → Consumer receives message
                              ↓
                        Processing fails
                              ↓
                   Message becomes visible again
                              ↓
                   Retry (up to maxReceiveCount times)
                              ↓
                   Moved to Dead Letter Queue
```

1. A consumer receives a message and attempts to process it
2. If the handler fails (throws an error), the message is not deleted
3. After the visibility timeout, the message becomes visible again
4. This repeats up to `maxReceiveCount` times
5. After exceeding the retry limit, the message is moved to the DLQ

## Worker with DLQ

The `QueueWorker` integrates naturally with DLQ. Failed messages are automatically retried:

```typescript
const q = rinda.queue(queue.id);

const worker = q.createWorker({
  handler: async (message) => {
    const order = message.body;

    if (!order.id) {
      throw new Error('Invalid order — missing ID');
      // Message becomes visible again after visibility timeout
      // After maxReceiveCount failures, moves to DLQ
    }

    await processOrder(order);
    return message; // Acknowledge
  },
  visibilityTimeout: 30,
});

worker.start();
```

## Monitoring Dead Letters

Use message introspection to view dead-lettered messages:

```typescript
const q = rinda.queue('QUEUE_ID');

const result = await q.inspect({
  status: 'DEAD_LETTERED',
  limit: 50,
});

for (const msg of result.data) {
  console.log(`Failed message: ${msg.providerMessageId}`);
  console.log(`  Receive count: ${msg.receiveCount}`);
  console.log(`  Error: ${msg.errorMessage}`);
}
```

## Redriving

Once you have fixed whatever made the messages fail, redrive them: they go
back on the queue and are delivered again.

```typescript
const q = rinda.queue('QUEUE_ID');

const result = await q.redrive();
console.log(`Moved ${result.moved} messages back onto the queue`);
```

Redriven messages get a fresh set of attempts. Without that reset each one
would arrive carrying the delivery count that dead-lettered it, and the first
failure after redriving would send it straight back — one attempt instead of
the queue's full allowance.

### Draining a large backlog

One call moves at most 500 messages and tells you whether there are more:

```typescript
let moved = 0;
let result;

do {
  result = await q.redrive();
  moved += result.moved;
} while (result.hasMore);

console.log(`Redrove ${moved} messages`);
```

The cap is there so a single request cannot stay open for as long as a large
backlog takes to move.

### Moving a few at a time

Pass `maxMessages` to redrive part of the backlog — useful when you want to
watch the first few succeed before releasing the rest:

```typescript
const result = await q.redrive({ maxMessages: 10 });
```

### What happens if a redrive fails partway

A message is put back on the queue before it is removed from the dead-letter
queue. If the second step fails, the message stays on the dead-letter queue
and the next redrive moves it again — so a redrive can deliver a message
twice, but cannot lose one.

Handlers should be idempotent for this reason, as they should be for any queue
delivery.

Messages that could not be moved are reported separately and left where they
were:

```typescript
const result = await q.redrive();

if (result.failed > 0) {
  console.warn(`${result.failed} could not be moved — they are still on the DLQ`);
}
```

### Redriving from the dashboard

A queue with a dead-letter queue has a **Redrive** button on its overview
page, showing how many messages are waiting. It drains the whole backlog,
making as many calls as that takes.

## Best Practices

1. **Always enable DLQ for production queues** — prevents poison messages from blocking processing
2. **Set appropriate retry counts** — 3-5 retries is typical for most workloads
3. **Monitor your DLQ** — set up alerts when messages arrive in the DLQ
4. **Investigate root causes** — use message introspection to understand why messages failed
5. **Redrive when fixed** — once the issue is resolved, call `redrive()` to put the messages back
6. **Fix before you redrive** — a message that fails again returns to the DLQ, so redriving into an unfixed bug just moves the backlog back and forth

---

# Environments

Rinda environments provide isolated contexts for your queues and storage, ensuring safe separation between development, staging, and production.

## Default Environments

Every project comes with three environments:

| Environment | API Key Prefix | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Development | `rk_dev_...` | Local development and testing |
| Staging | `rk_stg_...` | Pre-production validation |
| Production | `rk_prod_...` | Live traffic |

## How Isolation Works

- Each environment has its own set of **queues** and **storage objects**
- API keys are scoped to a single environment
- A production API key **cannot** access staging or development queues
- Queue names can be reused across environments (e.g., `order-events` in both dev and prod)

## Using Environments

Your code doesn't need to know which environment it's running in — the API key determines the environment:

```typescript

// In development: uses dev queues
// In production: uses prod queues
// Determined entirely by the API key
const rinda = new Rinda({
  apiKey: process.env.RINDA_API_KEY,
});
```

## Environment Variables Setup

```bash
# .env.development
RINDA_API_KEY=rk_dev_abc123

# .env.staging
RINDA_API_KEY=rk_stg_def456

# .env.production
RINDA_API_KEY=rk_prod_ghi789
```

## Best Practices

1. **Never use production keys locally** — always use development keys for local work
2. **Use separate API keys per service** — easier to rotate and audit
3. **Match infrastructure** — keep queue configurations similar across environments
4. **Test in staging first** — validate changes before deploying to production

---

# Message Introspection

Message introspection lets you view the full lifecycle of messages flowing through your queues — from sent to processed, failed, or dead-lettered. It is invaluable for debugging and monitoring.

## Inspecting Messages

Filter and paginate messages with `inspect`:

```typescript
const q = rinda.queue('QUEUE_ID');

const result = await q.inspect({
  status: 'FAILED',
  limit: 50,
});

console.log(`Found ${result.data.length} failed messages`);
for (const msg of result.data) {
  console.log(`${msg.providerMessageId}: ${msg.errorMessage}`);
}

// Pagination
if (result.pagination.hasMore) {
  const nextPage = await q.inspect({
    status: 'FAILED',
    cursor: result.pagination.nextCursor,
  });
}
```

### Filter Options

| Filter | Description |
|---|---|
| `status` | Filter by lifecycle status |
| `groupId` | Filter by FIFO message group |
| `deduplicationId` | Filter by deduplication ID |
| `search` | Text search in message body |
| `cursor` | Pagination cursor from previous response |
| `limit` | Max results (default: 50, max: 100) |

## Message Statuses

| Status | Description |
|---|---|
| `QUEUED` | Message is in the queue, waiting to be received |
| `PROCESSING` | Message has been received and is being processed |
| `PROCESSED` | Message was successfully processed and deleted |
| `FAILED` | Message processing failed (will be retried) |
| `DEAD_LETTERED` | Message exceeded max retries and was moved to DLQ |
| `DELETED` | Message was explicitly deleted |
| `EXPIRED` | Message exceeded retention period |
| `DEDUPLICATED` | Duplicate message was suppressed |

## Full-Text Search

Search messages by body content using PostgreSQL full-text search:

```typescript
const result = await q.search('order-123', 20);

console.log(`Found ${result.data.length} matching messages`);
for (const msg of result.data) {
  console.log(`${msg.providerMessageId}: ${msg.status}`);
}
```

## Message Groups (FIFO)

View message groups and their aggregated statistics for FIFO queues:

```typescript
const result = await q.groups(10);

for (const group of result.data) {
  console.log(`Group: ${group.groupId}`);
  console.log(`  Total: ${group.messageCount}`);
  console.log(`  Queued: ${group.queued}`);
  console.log(`  Processing: ${group.processing}`);
  console.log(`  Processed: ${group.processed}`);
  console.log(`  Failed: ${group.failed}`);
  console.log(`  Dead-lettered: ${group.deadLettered}`);
}
```

## Statistics

Get a high-level breakdown of message statuses:

```typescript
const result = await q.breakdown();

console.log('Message breakdown:');
for (const { status, count } of result.data.byStatus) {
  console.log(`  ${status}: ${count}`);
}
console.log('Total deduplicated:', result.data.totalDeduplicated);
```

## Use Cases

- **Debugging** — Find out why a specific message failed
- **Monitoring** — Track message throughput and failure rates
- **Auditing** — Full message lifecycle for compliance
- **Alerting** — Detect message processing issues early

---
